title: Subtitles on the rise
text: For decades, English-speaking audiences treated subtitles as a chore; now they {{1}} them on as a matter of routine. Streaming is the obvious cause — a series from Seoul or Oslo {{2}} in every territory at once, and audiences quickly {{3}} that a good subtitle disappears as completely as a good dub. The craft behind that invisibility is stricter than most viewers {{4}}: a subtitle may hold no more than about forty characters a line, must stay on screen long enough to read, and cannot {{5}} every word — dialogue that takes four seconds is compressed to what fits in four seconds, which is why screen subtitles read {{6}} from the script. Fans debate the rest with professional {{7}}: whether names should be adapted or transliterated, whether songs should be translated at all, and whether translator's notes belong on screen. What once took a {{8}} of specialists in a single city now happens in dozens of languages within days of release — an unglamorous, invisible industry without which the globalisation of television simply would not run.

gaps.explanation: 'switch them on as a matter of routine' — the phrasal verb for activating; sketch = draw roughly.
'a series premieres in every territory at once' — has its first showing; premier = prime minister; permeate = spread through.
'audiences quickly discover that…' — find out; discard = throw away.
'stricter than most viewers appreciate' — realise properly; apprehend = arrest or grasp mentally.
'cannot fit every word' — get it into the limited space; fill every word is not idiomatic.
'subtitles read differently from the script' — 'read differently from' is the pattern; indifferent = unconcerned.
'debate with professional rigour' — professional strictness; rigmarole = a lengthy, confusing procedure.
'a handful of specialists' — only a few; hindrance = an obstruction.
